questions.title: What three pieces define an Angular component?
explanation: A component has a TypeScript class for behavior, a template describing rendered DOM, and a selector identifying its host element. The @Component metadata connects them and declares imports, styles, providers, and change-detection options.

questions.title: What does standalone-by-default mean for modern Angular components?
explanation: Modern components can be imported directly by other components without declaration in an NgModule. Older non-standalone declarations remain supported, but standalone imports make dependencies local and simplify lazy loading and composition.

questions.title: Why should component selectors normally use a project-specific prefix?
explanation: A consistent prefix reduces collisions with native elements and third-party components and makes ownership visible in templates. Custom element selectors should include a hyphen and avoid the reserved ng prefix.

questions.title: What is the difference between a component's host element and its view?
explanation: The host is the DOM element matched by the component selector. The view is the DOM Angular renders from that component's template inside the host; host bindings configure the outer host itself.

questions.title: When should host bindings be declared in component metadata?
explanation: Use host metadata to bind host classes, attributes, properties, or events that are part of the component contract. Prefer it over decorating many fields when the host behavior can be expressed clearly in one metadata object.

questions.title: How do interpolation and property binding differ?
explanation: Interpolation converts an expression to text within content or an attribute-like value. Property binding assigns the expression result to a DOM, directive, or component property and preserves non-string types.

source.title: Binding Dynamic Text, Properties and Attributes

questions.title: Why must an ARIA value often use attribute binding?
explanation: ARIA values are attributes rather than matching DOM element properties. attr.aria-label tells Angular to set or remove the attribute, whereas binding a nonexistent ariaLabel property can fail or behave incorrectly.

questions.title: What does Angular template expression context contain?
explanation: Expressions can read component members, template variables, and contextual variables introduced by control-flow blocks. They support a safe subset of JavaScript and should remain brief calculations rather than perform hidden side effects.

questions.title: How does @if differ from hiding an element with CSS?
explanation: @if conditionally creates or destroys its rendered view, affecting component lifecycle, subscriptions, and DOM cost. CSS hiding leaves the element and component alive, which is appropriate only when state and semantics should remain mounted.

questions.title: Why is tracking by object identity fragile in an @for block?
explanation: A refetch or immutable update may create new object instances for unchanged logical rows, making Angular recreate DOM and child state. Track a stable unique property such as item.id whenever the data model provides one.

source.title: Why is track in @for Blocks Important?

questions.title: When is $index an acceptable @for tracking key?
explanation: It is acceptable for a truly static list whose items are never inserted, removed, reordered, or filtered. Dynamic collections need stable data identity to preserve the right DOM and component state.

questions.title: What problem does ng-container solve?
explanation: ng-container groups template behavior, directives, outlets, or conditional content without adding a real DOM element. This preserves layout and semantics while providing an Angular composition point.

questions.title: How does ng-template differ from ordinary template markup?
explanation: ng-template declares a TemplateRef that is not rendered at its declaration location by default. Angular can instantiate it through control flow, an outlet, or a view container with an explicit context.

questions.title: When should content projection use multiple select slots?
explanation: Use selectors when a component accepts distinct semantic regions such as a card title, body, and actions. Define a fallback where useful and avoid conditionally adding ng-content because projection slots are established at compile time.

questions.title: What is the difference between a component and an attribute directive?
explanation: A component owns a template and host view. An attribute directive adds behavior to an existing host element without creating its own template, making it suitable for reusable interaction or presentation behavior.

questions.title: How should writable signal state be updated from its current value?
explanation: update receives the current signal value and returns the next one, which avoids reading and setting in separate code. For object values, return a new object when identity-based consumers need to observe the change.

questions.title: Why should a computed signal not perform side effects?
explanation: A computed value is a lazy memoized derivation that Angular may reevaluate according to dependency changes. Side effects make that evaluation order observable and can create loops; keep computed pure and use explicit event logic or carefully scoped effects for synchronization.

questions.title: How do computed signal dependencies change dynamically?
explanation: Angular tracks only signals read during the latest computation. Conditional branches can add or remove dependencies, so changing an unread signal does not invalidate the computed value until that branch becomes active.

questions.title: Why can mutating an array inside a signal fail to update the view?
explanation: Mutation keeps the same reference, and the signal's equality check may consider the value unchanged. Use set or update to return a new array, preserving a clear immutable state transition.

questions.title: What does untracked do inside reactive signal code?
explanation: untracked allows reading a signal without recording it as a dependency of the current computed or effect. Use it only when the value is incidental and must not trigger reevaluation, not to hide a real dependency.

questions.title: When is linkedSignal preferable to an effect that resets another signal?
explanation: linkedSignal models writable state derived from another reactive source and updates it when that source changes. It expresses the dependency directly and avoids using an effect for state propagation, while still allowing user changes between source updates.

questions.title: What lifecycle does a signal effect have?
explanation: An effect runs in an injection context, tracks signal reads, and reruns when those dependencies change. It is normally destroyed with its enclosing context, and registered cleanup can cancel work before reruns or final destruction.

questions.title: Why can signal effects create circular updates?
explanation: If an effect reads one signal and writes another that eventually changes the first, reactive propagation can cycle or produce unstable state. Model derived values with computed or linkedSignal and perform state changes at explicit event boundaries.

questions.title: How does reading a signal in an OnPush template schedule updates?
explanation: Angular registers the view as a consumer of the signal. When the signal changes, Angular marks the component for checking, providing an explicit notification compatible with OnPush and zoneless change detection.

questions.title: What is the difference between input() and a traditional @Input?
explanation: The input function declares a signal-based input read by calling it and supports required inputs, transforms, and aliasing. Decorator inputs remain supported, but signal inputs compose directly with computed state and reactive templates.

questions.title: Why use a required signal input?
explanation: input.required communicates that a parent must provide the value and enables compile-time template checking. It removes ambiguous undefined handling from the child when absence is not valid.

questions.title: What does model() add beyond a normal input?
explanation: A model input is writable by the child and automatically creates a matching change output for two-way binding. Use it when the child legitimately edits a value owned collaboratively with its parent, not for every input.

questions.title: How do output() events differ from DOM events?
explanation: Angular custom outputs emit typed values to template listeners and do not bubble through the DOM. Their names should describe domain events and avoid collisions with native event names.

questions.title: When should afterNextRender be used?
explanation: Use it for DOM work that must occur after Angular has rendered the application, such as measurement or integration setup. Unlike component lifecycle hooks, render callbacks are application-wide and do not run during server rendering.

questions.title: How does DestroyRef improve cleanup design?
explanation: DestroyRef lets code register cleanup close to resource setup and can be passed to helper functions. Its destroyed state also helps prevent delayed work from acting after the owning component or service has been destroyed.

questions.title: What is an Angular injection context?
explanation: It is a runtime context associated with an injector where inject() can resolve dependencies. Constructors, field initializers, provider factories, guards, and code run through runInInjectionContext are common examples.

questions.title: Why does inject() fail in an ordinary method called later?
explanation: A normal method invocation usually has no active injection context. Resolve the dependency in a field initializer or constructor, pass it as an argument, or deliberately execute setup through runInInjectionContext.

questions.title: What scope does providedIn: 'root' create?
explanation: It registers a tree-shakable provider with the application root environment injector, normally producing one shared instance for that application. Component-level providers can still create scoped overriding instances.

questions.title: When should a service be provided at component level?
explanation: Provide it on a component when each subtree needs isolated state or lifecycle, such as a wizard instance. Descendants share that scoped instance, and it is destroyed with the component injector.

questions.title: How do useClass, useValue, useFactory, and useExisting providers differ?
explanation: useClass constructs a type, useValue supplies a fixed value, useFactory computes a value from dependencies, and useExisting aliases another token without creating a second instance. Choose the form that makes scope and ownership explicit.

questions.title: Why is InjectionToken needed for an interface-shaped dependency?
explanation: TypeScript interfaces disappear at runtime, so Angular cannot use them as DI keys. An InjectionToken provides runtime identity and can carry a generic type plus an optional tree-shakable factory.

questions.title: How should environment configuration be injected?
explanation: Define a typed InjectionToken and provide a validated immutable value during bootstrap or platform integration. Components depend on the token rather than importing mutable global files, which improves testing and deployment substitution.

questions.title: What does a multi provider enable?
explanation: multi: true lets multiple providers contribute values under one token, and consumers inject the resulting array. It supports extension points such as validators, interceptors, or plugin registrations without one provider replacing another.

questions.title: Why can useExisting be preferable to useClass for an alias?
explanation: useExisting returns the same instance registered under another token. useClass creates a separate instance, which can duplicate state and lifecycle when the intent was merely another name.

questions.title: How does provider shadowing work in Angular's injector hierarchy?
explanation: Resolution starts at the requesting element or environment injector and walks upward. A nearer provider for the same token shadows ancestor providers for that subtree while siblings continue using their own resolution path.

questions.title: When should optional injection be used?
explanation: Use optional injection when absence is a supported mode with a clear fallback, often in reusable infrastructure. Do not mark required business dependencies optional merely to hide configuration errors.

questions.title: What problem can a DI circular dependency indicate?
explanation: Two services requiring each other often reveal mixed responsibilities or an implicit event cycle. Extract a lower-level abstraction, invert one dependency with a token, or coordinate through explicit state rather than using delayed lookup as the default fix.

questions.title: How should a service with an external resource clean up?
explanation: Tie subscriptions, observers, workers, or sockets to the provider's actual injector lifetime using DestroyRef or an explicit dispose contract. Root services live for the application, while scoped providers can be destroyed with their route or component.

questions.title: What makes a reactive form model explicit?
explanation: FormControl, FormGroup, and FormArray objects define values, validation, status, and update behavior in TypeScript. This makes complex dynamic forms easier to compose, test, and inspect than deriving the whole model from template directives.

questions.title: Why should a FormGroup use setValue differently from patchValue?
explanation: setValue requires a complete value matching the group's structure and catches missing fields. patchValue updates only supplied descendants, which is useful for partial data but can silently ignore an accidental omission.

source.title: Updating Parts of the Data Model

questions.title: How should cross-field form validation be implemented?
explanation: Attach a validator to the common FormGroup so it can compare sibling controls and return a group-level error. The template can show that error after suitable interaction without duplicating business logic in event handlers.

questions.title: Why must asynchronous validators complete?
explanation: Angular uses the emitted result and completion to finalize validation status. An observable that never completes can leave the control pending; use a finite request stream and handle transport errors as a defined validation outcome.

questions.title: When should updateOn be set to blur or submit?
explanation: Use blur or submit to reduce expensive validation and network work or to avoid noisy feedback during typing. The choice affects value and status timing, so tests and UX must reflect the selected interaction model.

questions.title: How does ControlValueAccessor integrate a custom form control?
explanation: It bridges Angular Forms and a custom UI by writing model values, registering change and touched callbacks, and handling disabled state. The component must avoid emitting a change merely because Angular wrote a value.

questions.title: Why can nested subscriptions create stale HTTP results?
explanation: Each outer emission starts an independent inner subscription, so older responses can arrive after newer ones and cleanup becomes scattered. switchMap cancels the previous inner request when only the latest query matters.

questions.title: When should switchMap, concatMap, mergeMap, or exhaustMap be chosen for an HTTP action?
explanation: Choose from concurrency semantics: switchMap keeps the latest, concatMap queues in order, mergeMap runs concurrently, and exhaustMap ignores new triggers while one runs. Match that behavior to search, sequential writes, parallel independent work, or duplicate-submit prevention.

questions.title: How does AsyncPipe manage an observable subscription?
explanation: AsyncPipe subscribes, returns the latest value, marks the view for checking on emissions, switches when the source reference changes, and unsubscribes when destroyed. It is usually safer than manual template-facing subscriptions.

questions.title: What does takeUntilDestroyed solve?
explanation: It completes an observable subscription when the current injection context is destroyed, removing manual Subject boilerplate. A DestroyRef can be passed explicitly when the call occurs outside an injection context.

questions.title: How do toSignal and toObservable bridge Angular and RxJS?
explanation: toSignal subscribes to an Observable and exposes its latest value as a Signal with lifecycle and initial-value considerations. toObservable exposes signal changes through an Observable so RxJS composition can consume them.

questions.title: Why is HttpClient Observable execution called cold?
explanation: Each subscription starts a separate request, so multiple subscriptions can duplicate network work. Share or cache deliberately when consumers should use one result, while defining invalidation and error behavior.

questions.title: Why should an HTTP interceptor clone a request before changing it?
explanation: HttpRequest instances are mostly immutable so retries and interceptor ordering remain predictable. clone creates a modified request while preserving the original.

questions.title: What should an interceptor avoid?
explanation: Avoid UI-specific business logic, unbounded retries, swallowing errors, and mutable global request state. Interceptors are best for cross-cutting transport concerns such as authentication, tracing, deadlines, caching policy, and consistent error translation.

questions.title: How should HTTP errors be modeled for components?
explanation: Translate transport failures into a small application error model with safe codes, retryability, and user-facing intent. Keep raw backend payloads and stack details out of templates while retaining correlation data for diagnostics.

questions.title: What is the difference between RouterLink and calling router.navigate?
explanation: RouterLink declaratively generates accessible navigation in templates and handles URL creation. router.navigate is appropriate for imperative navigation after an event or workflow decision; normal links should remain links.

questions.title: How do route parameters differ from query parameters?
explanation: Route parameters identify a matched path segment and usually define resource identity. Query parameters add optional filtering, sorting, pagination, or view state and can persist across different navigation strategies.

questions.title: When should a route resolver be used?
explanation: Use a resolver when navigation should wait for essential route data and the product has a deliberate loading and error strategy. Avoid blocking navigation for optional or progressively loadable information.

questions.title: Why can a resolver make navigation feel frozen?
explanation: Navigation does not complete until resolver work emits and completes. A slow or never-completing stream delays the route, so apply finite requests, timeouts or error handling, and expose navigation progress.

questions.title: What does canMatch enable beyond canActivate?
explanation: canMatch decides whether a route configuration is eligible to match, allowing the router to consider another matching route when it returns false. canActivate runs after matching to decide whether activation may proceed.

questions.title: Why should a guard return a UrlTree instead of calling navigate and returning false?
explanation: Returning a UrlTree or redirect command makes redirection part of the same navigation decision and avoids overlapping navigations. It is easier for the router to coordinate, cancel, and test.

questions.title: How should route-level code splitting be designed?
explanation: Lazy-load feature routes or standalone components at meaningful navigation boundaries, keep shared eager code small, and measure real chunk waterfalls. Over-fragmentation adds requests, while one large lazy chunk delays the feature.

questions.title: What is a preloading strategy used for?
explanation: It loads selected lazy route code after initial navigation so future transitions are faster. Choose based on network, device, user intent, and bundle cost rather than preloading every feature unconditionally.

questions.title: When should nested routes use a child router outlet?
explanation: Use children when a feature layout remains mounted while its inner content changes. The parent component hosts an outlet, and child URLs express the hierarchy and preserve shared navigation or state.

questions.title: What problem does route title configuration solve?
explanation: Static or resolved route titles keep document titles aligned with navigation and improve accessibility, history, and sharing. A custom TitleStrategy can centralize application prefixes and hierarchical rules.

questions.title: How should unsaved form navigation be handled?
explanation: A canDeactivate guard may confirm or block in-app navigation based on dirty state, while browser beforeunload behavior needs separate limited handling. Persist drafts where loss would be severe and never rely on the guard for server authorization.

questions.title: Why can subscribing directly to ActivatedRoute in a reused component need switchMap?
explanation: The same component instance may receive new parameters without being recreated. switchMap cancels obsolete data requests when parameters change, preventing an older response from replacing the current route data.

questions.title: How should a not-found route be ordered?
explanation: Angular uses first-match-wins route configuration, so a wildcard fallback belongs after all specific routes. Placing it early captures valid URLs before they reach their intended route.

questions.title: What is the danger of storing sensitive state only in navigation extras?
explanation: Navigation state may be absent after refresh, direct linking, or a new tab, and client data is never a trusted security source. Put durable identity in the URL or server and reconstruct safe view state.

questions.title: How should router scroll restoration be evaluated?
explanation: Configure it according to product navigation expectations and test back/forward, fragments, dynamic content, and hydration. Restoring before content stabilizes can land at the wrong position, requiring coordination with rendering and data loading.

questions.title: What does Angular template sanitization protect against?
explanation: Angular treats bound values as untrusted and sanitizes or escapes according to HTML, style, URL, and resource-URL security contexts. Template and code construction still must avoid turning untrusted text into executable templates or trusted values.

questions.title: Why is bypassSecurityTrustHtml dangerous?
explanation: It tells Angular to trust a value and skip normal sanitization, so untrusted content can become executable markup. Use it only after a narrow, audited trust decision and keep the trust call close to the verified source.

questions.title: How does Content Security Policy complement Angular's defenses?
explanation: CSP limits which scripts, styles, and resources the browser may execute or load, reducing impact if markup injection occurs. Use nonces or hashes and Trusted Types where supported, test third-party dependencies, and avoid unsafe-inline exceptions.

questions.title: Why should authentication tokens not be logged by an interceptor?
explanation: Tokens are bearer credentials and logs are widely copied, indexed, and retained. Redact authorization and personal data, log bounded metadata and correlation identifiers, and apply access and retention controls.

questions.title: What does TestBed provide over constructing a component class directly?
explanation: TestBed compiles templates, resolves DI, creates a fixture, and exercises Angular binding and lifecycle behavior. Direct construction is faster for pure class logic that does not depend on framework integration.

questions.title: How should a component test trigger user behavior?
explanation: Interact through rendered DOM events and assert visible output or public effects, then allow Angular to stabilize. Directly calling private methods bypasses template bindings, event wiring, and accessibility behavior.

questions.title: Why should an HTTP test call verify after each test?
explanation: HttpTestingController.verify detects unexpected or unflushed requests, preventing a test from passing while leaving background work unresolved. Match request method, URL, body, and relevant headers before flushing a controlled response.

questions.title: Why must provideHttpClient come before provideHttpClientTesting?
explanation: The testing provider replaces parts of the normal HTTP setup with its mock backend. Reversing the order can overwrite the testing configuration and allow incorrect behavior or real requests.

questions.title: How should route behavior be tested?
explanation: Configure real test routes and use RouterTestingHarness to navigate, then assert URL, rendered component, guards, parameters, and error paths. Mocking Router internals can hide integration defects and framework changes.

questions.title: What should a component harness abstract?
explanation: A harness exposes stable user-meaningful operations and state for a component while hiding DOM implementation details. Library and design-system tests then survive markup refactoring while still exercising real rendered behavior.

questions.title: Why can fakeAsync be the wrong choice for some asynchronous tests?
explanation: fakeAsync controls supported timers and microtasks in its zone, but APIs outside that model or zoneless behavior may not match reality. Prefer async/await with fixture.whenStable when it represents production scheduling more faithfully.

questions.title: How should accessibility be tested in an Angular component library?
explanation: Test semantic elements, names, roles, keyboard behavior, focus management, states, and contrast with automated checks plus manual assistive-technology review. Preserve these contracts through harnesses and end-to-end workflows, not only snapshots.

questions.title: How do CSR, SSG, and SSR differ for Angular routes?
explanation: CSR renders in the browser, SSG creates route HTML at build time, and SSR creates HTML per request. Choose per route from SEO, freshness, personalization, build time, server cost, and interactivity needs.

questions.title: Why must server and client templates produce the same DOM for hydration?
explanation: Hydration matches existing server nodes to the client view, including Angular-created structure and relevant whitespace. Browser-only conditionals or direct DOM mutation can create mismatches, forcing errors or skipped hydration.

questions.title: When is ngSkipHydration acceptable?
explanation: It is a temporary escape hatch for a component whose direct DOM manipulation or incompatible library cannot hydrate. Apply it at a component host, measure the lost reuse, and plan to make the component hydration-compatible.

source.title: How to Skip Hydration for Particular Components

questions.title: What does event replay protect during hydration?
explanation: It captures supported user events that occur before hydration finishes and replays them after the relevant UI becomes interactive. This reduces lost early interactions but does not replace fast loading or correct server markup.

questions.title: What is incremental hydration?
explanation: It hydrates deferred regions according to configured triggers rather than activating the whole page at once. Combined with @defer, it can reduce initial client work while replaying interactions for not-yet-hydrated regions.

questions.title: How does @defer improve an Angular application's initial bundle?
explanation: Dependencies used only inside a defer block can be split into lazy chunks and loaded on triggers such as viewport, interaction, idle, or a condition. Placeholder, loading, and error blocks define the user experience around that work.

questions.title: Why can many immediate @defer blocks hurt performance?
explanation: They can create a burst of chunk requests and main-thread work after startup, shifting rather than removing cost. Group related dependencies, select intent-based triggers, prefetch carefully, and measure waterfalls on real devices.

questions.title: What must notify Angular to run change detection in a zoneless application?
explanation: Notifications include updating a signal read by a template, markForCheck, ComponentRef.setInput, template or host listeners, and attaching a marked view. Code relying only on ZoneJS task completion must adopt an explicit notification.

questions.title: Why is OnPush useful when migrating to zoneless Angular?
explanation: OnPush-compatible code already relies on explicit notifications such as inputs, signals, AsyncPipe, and markForCheck instead of global async patching. It exposes hidden mutable-state assumptions before ZoneJS is removed.

questions.title: Why can a zoneless test pass only after fixture.detectChanges and still be defective?
explanation: Manual detectChanges can mask that production code never notified Angular of a state update. Prefer changing state through signals, inputs, listeners, or markForCheck and await fixture.whenStable so the test follows production scheduling.

questions.title: How should Angular bundle budgets be used?
explanation: Set warning and error thresholds for initial and targeted bundles in angular.json, then track them in CI. Budgets provide a regression gate, while bundle analysis identifies which dependencies, duplication, or eager features caused growth.

questions.title: What is the purpose of Angular's AOT compilation?
explanation: AOT compiles templates and metadata during the build, catches template errors earlier, and avoids shipping the template compiler for normal production execution. Production builds also apply bundling and optimization around the compiled output.

questions.title: How should an Angular service worker update be rolled out?
explanation: Treat the worker and application files as one versioned deployment, serve correct cache headers, detect available versions, and prompt or activate according to the risk of mixing old UI with new APIs. Provide recovery when cached assets become inconsistent.

questions.title: Why should browser globals be isolated in SSR-compatible code?
explanation: window, document, localStorage, and layout APIs may not exist or have the same meaning on the server. Use Angular abstractions, platform checks at narrow boundaries, and render-compatible initial state so server and client output agree.

questions.title: What production evidence should guide an Angular performance change?
explanation: Measure Core Web Vitals, route and chunk waterfalls, change-detection cost, long tasks, memory, server render time, and hydration behavior on representative devices. Use Angular DevTools and browser profiles, change the measured bottleneck, then verify the user-facing improvement and accessibility.
